title: Reverse a String in Place
statement:
C++ passes function arguments by value unless you say otherwise: a
`std::string` parameter taken by value is a full copy, and anything the
function does to its own copy is invisible to the caller the moment the
function returns. A `std::string&` parameter -- a reference -- is the
opposite: there is only ever one string, and the parameter is simply
another name for it, so a change made through the parameter *is* a change
to the caller's own variable.

## Your function

```
void ReverseInPlace(std::string& text);
```

Reverse `text` in place, so that the caller's own string reads backwards
afterwards. `text` may be empty. Return nothing -- the whole point is that
the caller sees the change through the reference, not through a return
value.

## Watch out

- **A `std::string` parameter (no `&`) would compile and run without ever
  changing anything the caller can see.** Reversing a *copy* is legal C++
  and produces exactly the wrong observable result: the function appears
  to do nothing at all, because "nothing at all" and "reversed a copy that
  was thrown away at the end of the function" look identical from the
  caller's side.
- **An empty string, and a one-character string, need no swaps at all.** A
  loop that walks two indices toward each other from both ends has to stop
  before they cross or meet, or it will read (and swap) past the string's
  own bounds.
- `text[i]` gives you a `char&` -- a reference to the character itself, not
  a copy of it -- so `std::swap(text[i], text[j])` really does exchange
  the two characters in the caller's string, the same reference idea one
  level down.

tests.name: an empty string reverses to itself
a palindrome reverses to itself
